section_summaries.epidemiology: Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is the most common parasitic infection of the brain and a major cause of adult-onset epilepsy worldwide, endemic in most non-Muslim developing countries across South/Central America, Asia, and Africa. Prevalence varies based on animal husbandry, hygiene, and dietary practices, with approximately 30% of seizure disorders in endemic areas attributed to NCC. Industrialized practices have reduced local propagation, but cases arise in high-income countries due to immigration and travel to endemic regions, such as outbreaks among immigrant tapeworm carriers.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Cysticercosis occurs when humans ingest Taenia solium tapeworm eggs from fecally contaminated material, becoming intermediate hosts where cysticerci develop in tissues, similar to pigs. Autoinfection or person-to-person transmission through unhygienic food preparation is possible. Living cysticerci actively evade the host's immune system, especially in immunologically privileged sites like the brain and eyes, typically causing minimal inflammation. Symptoms usually arise from inflammation caused by dying cysticerci, explaining the delay between infection and symptom onset (3 months to several years). Inflammation, characterized by lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, and conspicuous eosinophils, can be asymptomatic or fatal, leading to granuloma, fibrous scar, or calcification. In the CNS, two main forms exist: spherical/ovoid parenchymal or ventricular cysticerci (5-10 mm, containing a scolex), and uncommon large, lobulated, vesicular 'racemose cysticercosis' in basal cisternal spaces, which lack a scolex and represent a late degenerative form or different anatomical response.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Cysticerci can infect any tissue, but clinically significant lesions primarily involve the brain, spinal cord (Neurocysticercosis, NCC), or the eye. Clinical features depend on the number, size, location, stage of evolution, and inflammatory response. Intraparenchymal NCC frequently causes seizures, often focal with secondary generalization, potentially accompanied by focal encephalitis and edema. Extraparenchymal NCC (intraventricular or subarachnoid) is linked to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) with or without hydrocephalus, basal arachnoiditis, cranial nerve palsies, vasculitis, cerebral infarcts, and obstructive hydrocephalus. The encephalitic form, common in children and young females, involves massive brain infection with severe edema, ICP, seizures, and reduced consciousness. Spinal cysticercosis, usually subarachnoid, and ophthalmic cysticercosis, typically retinal or subretinal, can threaten vision through inflammation. Muscular and subcutaneous cysticerci present as palpable, pea-like nodules, usually asymptomatic but sometimes painful during degeneration.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis of NCC is suspected in patients with neurologic symptoms and a history of living in or traveling in endemic regions, especially with late-onset seizures or raised ICP, and is based on neuroimaging and serology. Brain imaging (CT or MRI) is crucial: living cysticerci appear as 5-10 mm hypodense lesions without contrast enhancement; degenerating cysts show edema and ring/nodular enhancement; end-stage calcified cysts are hyperdense. MRI is superior for living/degenerating cysts and edema but less sensitive for calcifications, which can also be seen on plain radiographs of muscles. Serology, specifically enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) using lentil-lectin purified glycoprotein antigens, is the assay of choice for infection-specific antibodies in serum or CSF, offering >98% sensitivity/specificity (though 60-80% for single lesions). Antigen detection ELISA may monitor extraparenchymal disease. Stool examination for Taenia spp. eggs or expelled proglottids helps identify intestinal tapeworm carriers; PCR is more accurate for species identification. Biopsy of subcutaneous nodules provides definitive diagnosis by revealing a fluid-filled bladder with a larval tapeworm scolex.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment for neurocysticercosis is individualized, combining symptomatic and anti-parasitic therapies. Symptomatic management includes analgesics, anti-convulsants, anti-inflammatory drugs (corticosteroids, especially for raised ICP or persistent inflammation), and ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion for hydrocephalus. Anti-parasitic therapy with albendazole (15 mg/kg/day for 8-15 days) or praziquantel (50-75 mg/kg/day for 15 days) targets living parasites, improving seizure evolution; albendazole is preferred for its efficacy and cost. Concurrent corticosteroids are given to manage inflammation and intracranial hypertension that can occur when larvae die during anti-parasitic treatment. Asymptomatic viable cysticerci are generally not treated, as they often resolve spontaneously. Ocular cysticercosis is typically treated surgically to prevent permanent vision loss, with cestocidal drugs, cryotherapy, or photocoagulation under investigation. Asymptomatic subcutaneous or intramuscular cysticerci usually do not require treatment, but symptomatic ones may be excised or treated with cestocidal drugs and anti-inflammatory agents.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention of cysticercosis focuses on interrupting the Taenia solium life cycle. Human infection with tapeworms can be prevented by adequately freezing or cooking pork. Human cysticercosis, which results from fecal-oral contamination with T. solium eggs, is prevented through basic hygiene and sanitation. T. solium is considered a potentially eradicable disease, with evidence supporting focal elimination through intervention programs in endemic regions.
